title: SI quantities, prefixes, and engineering notation
objective: Identify quantity and unit roles, interpret case-sensitive SI prefixes, and convert exact values between scientific, engineering, and prefixed notation.
why: A prefix or unit error can change a circuit quantity by a million while leaving the arithmetic looking reasonable. Keep the numerical value, unit size, and physical quantity separate so that a calculator result has a clear meaning.

sections.heading: Quick recall
paragraphs: A quantity value is a number multiplied by a unit. Prefixes change unit size by exact powers of ten. To convert between prefixes, multiply the numerical value by $10^{e_{source}-e_{target}}$. The physical quantity stays the same.

Scientific notation uses $1\leq |a|<10$ in $a\times10^n$ for a nonzero value. Our engineering convention uses an exponent divisible by three and $1\leq |a|<1000$. If these rules are familiar, try the examples and checkpoint; use the remaining explanations when a step feels uncertain.

sections.heading: A number needs a quantity and a unit
paragraphs: In 2.4 kΩ, 2.4 is the numerical value, k is the prefix kilo, and Ω is the unit ohm. The quantity is resistance. The same resistance is 2400 Ω; its numerical value changed because the chosen unit became smaller. A unit tells you how a number is measured, while a quantity name tells you what is being measured.

The seven SI base units are metre m for length, kilogram kg for mass, second s for time, ampere A for electric current, kelvin K for thermodynamic temperature, mole mol for amount of substance, and candela cd for luminous intensity. Derived units combine base units. Charge is measured in coulombs, $1\,\mathrm C=1\,\mathrm{A\,s}$; current is measured in amperes. A current and a charge are different quantities even though both occur in circuits.

sections.heading: Prefixes are exact and case-sensitive
paragraphs: Common small prefixes are pico p ($10^{-12}$), nano n ($10^{-9}$), micro μ ($10^{-6}$), milli m ($10^{-3}$), centi c ($10^{-2}$), and deci d ($10^{-1}$). Common large prefixes are kilo k ($10^3$), mega M ($10^6$), giga G ($10^9$), and tera T ($10^{12}$). The BIPM link supplies the full current table, including prefixes outside this refresher.

Case is part of the symbol: mV means millivolt, while MV means megavolt. Prefix symbols join unit symbols without a space; put a space between the number and unit, as in 5 mV. Unit symbols are not pluralized. Kilogram is the SI base unit of mass, but decimal mass prefixes attach to gram: milligram is mg, not mkg. Do not stack prefixes.

sections.heading: Convert by preserving the same quantity
paragraphs: Write the equality between units first. Since one nanofarad is one thousand picofarads, 3300 pF is 3.3 nF. A larger target unit requires a smaller number of those units. For a signed voltage or current, a positive conversion factor preserves the sign.

You can always pass through the unprefixed unit: replace the source prefix with its power of ten, then divide by the target prefix's power. Subtracting exponents is a compact form of this two-step process. Reverse the conversion as a check. If the magnitude changes in both directions, inspect the factor.

sections.heading: Notation communicates scale and precision
paragraphs: Scientific notation makes order of magnitude explicit; engineering notation often lines up with prefixes in steps of three. The number 0.000082 can be written as $8.2\times10^{-5}$ or $82\times10^{-6}$. Both represent the same value. Zero has no unique normalized scientific exponent; write its reported precision explicitly instead.

An exact unit conversion does not create or erase measurement information. A stated 0.0200 A has three significant figures under conventional decimal reporting and becomes 20.0 mA. Writing 20 mA alone can obscure that intent. Lesson four explains precision in detail; here, retain the supplied meaningful digits rather than treating a change of units as a new measurement.

examples.title: Read a resistance report
examples.prompt: Interpret 2.4 kΩ and distinguish current from charge.

steps.reason: Replace the exact prefix while keeping the resistance quantity.
Current multiplied by elapsed time gives charge; their units are not interchangeable.

examples.conclusion: The resistance is 2400 Ω. An ampere measures current, while a coulomb measures charge.

examples.title: Respect the case of a prefix

steps.reason: The common volt unit cancels and exponents subtract.

examples.conclusion: One megavolt is one billion millivolts. Capitalization cannot be discarded.

examples.title: Remove a micro prefix

steps.reason: Use the exact SI prefix factor.
The target unit is larger, so the numerical value becomes smaller.

examples.conclusion: The capacitance remains the same physical quantity.

examples.title: Convert between two small prefixes

steps.reason: Choose the ratio that cancels the source unit.

examples.conclusion: The factor is 10^-3 on the numerical value. Conversion alone does not settle how many digits in an ambiguous integer report were measured.

examples.title: Choose scientific or engineering notation

steps.reason: Move the decimal to make the coefficient at least 1 and less than 10.
For engineering notation move the exponent to a multiple of three and compensate in the coefficient.

examples.conclusion: Scientific and engineering forms encode the same voltage with different normalization rules.

examples.title: Preserve meaningful trailing zeros
examples.prompt: Convert a reported 0.0200 A to mA.

steps.reason: The factor 1000 is exact, so it does not limit measurement precision.
The coefficient shows the three meaningful digits clearly.

examples.conclusion: Report 20.0 mA to preserve the supplied precision.

guided.title: Finish the reasoning
guided.setup: A capacitor is labeled 6.8 nF. Convert it to F and pF, then compare mega with milli.
before: Write nano as 10^-9 and pico as 10^-12.
Use source exponent minus target exponent for the numerical factor.

question.prompt: Convert 6.8 nF to F and pF. Also give the ratio (1 MV)/(1 mV).
hints: Write the supplied quantities and their units first.
Use source exponent minus target exponent for the numerical factor.
6.8 nF is 6.8 times 10^-9 F, or 6800 pF.
explanation: 6.8 nF is 6.8 times 10^-9 F, or 6800 pF.
question.answerSummary: 6.8 nF is 6.8 times 10^-9 F, or 6800 pF. Mega divided by milli is 10^6/10^-3=10^9.

guided.after: Explain each conversion before starting independent practice. Guided feedback is assisted work, not checkpoint evidence.

interaction.prompt: Choose a numerical value and two prefixes. Predict the converted value and factor exponent, then inspect the scale table and reverse conversion. Explain why changing the unit size preserves the physical quantity.

summary: A quantity equals a numerical value times a unit; changing units preserves the quantity.
Prefixes are exact and case-sensitive. Compare source and target exponents.
Scientific and engineering notation have different normalization rules; retain stated measurement precision.
retrieval: From memory convert 47 μA to A and mA. Explain why the numerical value grows when the unit becomes smaller, and why 47 MA would describe a different current.
